column2: But Karna, by fortitude suppressing that unbearable pain, bore it without trembling or flinching, holding the Bhargava.
Alas, I am made impure! What is this you are doing? Tell me, casting off fear, truly.
Karna then told him of the worm feeding on him, and Rama saw that worm too, like a boar,
eight-legged, sharp-fanged, as if covered with needles, its limbs bristling with hair, named Alarka.
As soon as Rama saw it, the worm gave up its life; and as its blood flowed, a wonder, as it were, occurred.
Then a Rakshasa of universal form was seen in the sky, fearsome, red-necked, black-limbed, cloud-borne.
With joined palms to Rama, his mind full, he said: "Good fortune to you, tiger of the Bhrigus; I shall go as I came.
I have been freed from hell by you, best of sages; may it be well with you, and prosperity; you have done me a kindness."
The mighty-armed, glorious son of Jamadagni said to him: "Who are you, and why did you fall into hell? Tell me."
He said: "I was the great asura named Gritsa, in the age of the gods long ago, dear one, of the same age as Bhrigu.
I forcibly seized Bhrigu's beloved wife, and by the great sage's curse I fell to the earth as a worm.
In anger he said to me, your forefather: 'Eating urine and phlegm, you will go to a sinful hell.'
'May the curse end, Brahmana,' I said to him; and Bhrigu said to me, 'It will end with a Bhargava, Rama.'
I have reached this state; not well, good one; meeting you, I am freed from a sinful birth."
Having said this and bowed, the great asura went to Rama; but Rama, angry, said these words to Karna:
This is exceeding pain, fool; a Brahmana could never bear it; this is the fortitude of a kshatriya alone; let the truth be told.
Then Karna, afraid of a curse, appeasing him, said: "Know me, Bhargava, born of a charioteer, between Brahmana and kshatriya.
People on earth call me Radheya Karna; be gracious to me, Brahmana, Bhargava, who was greedy for weapons.
A father is a teacher, no doubt, one who gives knowledge of the Veda, lord; so I said 'Bhargava' as my lineage in your presence."
The best of the Bhrigus, angry, as if laughing, said to him as he lay fallen on the ground, distressed, trembling, with joined palms:

Because you have served me falsely here out of greed for weapons, therefore this Brahma weapon will not come to your mind, fool,
mahabharata:12:3.31	except at the time of your death, when meeting one equal to you; for Brahma never stays in one who is not a Brahmana.
mahabharata:12:3.32	Go now; there is no place for you here, a liar; no kshatriya on earth will be your equal in battle.
Thus addressed by Rama, he went away, as was just, and approaching Duryodhana said, "I have mastered weapons."
Then once the kings gathered at a svayamvara in the country of Kalinga, of King Chitrangada, O king.
There was a city named Rajapura, glorious, Bharata, and hundreds of kings came there for the maiden.
Hearing that all the kings were assembled there, Duryodhana went in a golden-limbed chariot with Karna.
Then when that great festival of the svayamvara began, the kings gathered for the maiden, best of kings.
Shishupala, Jarasandha, Bhishmaka, Vakra, Kapotaroma, Nila and the firm-valiant Rukmi,
Srigala, great king, and the lord of the women's kingdom, Ashoka, Shatadhanva and the hero named Bhoja,
these and many others who lived in the southern region, and kings who were teachers of barbarians, from the east and north, Bharata,
all wearing golden armlets, with Jambunada garlands bound, all of shining bodies like tigers mad with rut.
But Duryodhana the Kaurava could not bear the transgression and, disregarding the kings, forbade that maiden.
Mad with pride of strength, relying on Bhishma and Drona, he lifted the maiden onto his chariot and challenged the kings.
Karna followed him, chariot-borne, sword in hand, with his iguana-skin fingerguard tied, best of weapon-bearers, behind, bull among men.
Then a great clash of the kings, Yudhishthira, took place, as they armed in armour and yoked chariots.
They rushed at both Karna and Duryodhana, enraged, loosing showers of arrows like clouds on two mountains.
Karna, as they came on, with a razor-arrow felled each one's bow with its quiver to the ground.
Some he left bowless, some with bows raised, some bearing arrows, chariot-spears and maces.
By his agility Karna, best of strikers, harassed them and conquered many kings, killing their charioteers.
Themselves urging their horses, saying "Go, go," those kings, their pride broken, left the battle.
Duryodhana, protected by Karna, then went glad, taking the maiden, to the city called Nagasahvaya.
A battle took place between the two, skilled in divine weapons, as they showered each other with weapons of many kinds.
With arrows spent, bowless, swords broken, both fell to the ground and grappled with their arms, both full of strength.
In arm-thorn fighting, Karna broke the joint of his body as he fought, he who was joined to old age.
Seeing the change in his body, the king said to Karna, "I am pleased," giving up enmity, Bharata.
In affection he gave Karna the city of Malini; he became king in Anga, bull among men, conqueror of foes.
Karna, crusher of strong foes, ruled Champa, with Duryodhana's approval, as you also know.
Thus by the power of his weapons he became famous on earth; for your benefit, Indra begged from him his armour and earrings.
Deluded by the god's illusion, he gave the divine, highly honoured innate earrings and the innate armour.
Freed of the earrings and the natural armour, he was slain in battle by Vijaya in the sight of Vasudeva,
by the curse of the Brahmana and of the great-souled Rama, by Kunti's boon, and by the illusion of Shatakratu,
by Bhishma's slighting in the reckoning of chariot-warriors, by the diminution of his energy by Shalya, and by Vasudeva's policy,
taking the divine weapons of Rudra, the king of the gods, Yama, Varuna, Kubera, Drona and the great-souled Kripa,
Karna son of Vikartana, bright as the sun, was slain in battle by the wielder of Gandiva.
Thus cursed and cheated by many, your brother, that tiger among men, is not to be grieved for, for he met death in battle."

Yudhishthira, mighty-armed, you ought not to grieve for him; cast off grief, greatly wise one, and hear this word of mine.

Thus addressed by his mother, the king of dharma, his eyes filled with tears, spoke, righteous, his mind distraught with grief:
I am wronged by your keeping the secret, he said to her, and, very greatly grieved, the greatly radiant one cursed women in all the worlds: "They will not keep a secret."
The king, remembering his sons, grandsons, relatives and friends, was agitated at heart and unsettled in mind.
Then, his soul filled with grief, like fire in smoke, the wise king, tormented, grew disgusted with the world.
[Yudhishthira said:] Overcome by grief and sorrow, sighing again and again, seeing Arjuna he said, wasted by grief:

The alms we shall seek in the cities of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, having left our kinsmen without men, will save us from this evil fate.

Having said this much, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, fell silent, and then Partha, the younger, replied.
[Arjuna said:] Showing himself fierce, of fierce valour, Indra's son (Arjuna), smiling, the greatly radiant, licking the corners of his mouth again and again, said:

Alas, what sorrow, what hardship, what supreme weakness, that having done superhuman deeds you would give up supreme fortune!

mahabharata:12:8.37	This path of prosperity is eternal; we have not heard of its end; great is the path of Dasharatha's son; do not take a bad road, O king.
[Yudhishthira said:] "I would never again go by a road to be travelled in company, because of you; I shall go, casting off the pleasures of village life.
Ask me: 'What road is safe for one to travel alone?' Or if you do not wish to ask, hear it from me unasked.
Casting off the pleasures and practices of village life, practising great austerity, I shall roam in the forest with the deer, eating fruit and roots,
offering oblations to the fire at due times, touching water at both twilights, lean, with limited food, wearing skin, bark and matted locks,
bearing cold, wind and heat, enduring hunger, thirst and toil, drying up my body by austerity as prescribed in the scriptures,
ever hearing high and low voices pleasant to mind and ear of the deer and birds living delighted in the forests,
smelling the pleasant fragrance of flowering trees and creepers, seeing in the forest the lovely forest-dwellers of many forms.
Even to the sight of the forest hermits who live in their families, I shall do nothing unpleasant, how much less to village dwellers.
Thus, following the ever sterner rule of the forest scriptures, I shall wait for the end of this body.
Or else I shall spend my days alone, going from tree to tree for a single day, begging, a shaven sage.
Covered in dust, dwelling in an empty house or at the root of a tree, having abandoned all likes and dislikes,
neither grieving nor rejoicing, regarding blame and self-praise as equal, without hope, without possessiveness, free of dualities, without possessions,
delighting in the Self, tranquil in soul, in the form of a dull, blind or deaf man, never making any agreement with anyone about anything,
harming none of the four kinds of beings, moving or unmoving, all creatures abiding in their dharma, equal toward all living beings,
not laughing at anyone, nowhere frowning, ever of a tranquil face, with all senses well controlled,
not asking anyone the way, going by whatever road, wishing to go to no particular place or direction,
indifferent in going, not looking behind, upright, composed, going, avoiding moving and unmoving beings,
his own nature goes ahead and foods come of themselves; thinking nothing of all the opposing pairs,
taking little or tasteless food, even when the first is not obtained; going to others too, filling seven by one gain in the absence of gain,
when the smoke is gone, the pestle laid down, the embers out, when people have eaten, when vessels have ceased to go about, when no beggars remain,
begging once a day, at two or five houses, I shall roam this earth, having freed myself from the nooses of desire.
Not like one wishing to live, nor like one wishing to die, neither welcoming life nor death nor hating them,
though one arm is cut with an adze and the other smeared with sandal, thinking neither ill nor good of either,
abandoning all activities of prosperity that can be done by one living, abiding by the winking of an eye (the moment),
ever unattached to them, with the activity of all senses abandoned, with intentions well abandoned, the soul's stain well washed,
freed from all attachments, passed beyond all snares, subject to no one, with the nature of the wind,
free of passion, thus roaming, I shall obtain eternal contentment; for through craving I have been led by ignorance to great sin.
